newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn has headache as GDP slows, joblessness rises.
newsitem.headline: Bonn has headache as GDP slows, joblessness rises.

text.p: Germany reported record joblessness and a slowdown in growth in Europe's biggest economy Thursday, giving Bonn a throbbing headache at the start of a year which is crucial to its bid to forge European monetary union.

The Federal Statistics Office said Germany's budget deficit rose to 3.9 percent of gross domestic product in 1996 from 3.5 percent in 1995, casting doubt on Bonn's pledge to reach the 3 percent ceiling set for nations seeking to merge their currencies into the Euro single currency in 1999.

GDP growth in 1996 slowed to 1.4 percent last year according to provisional data, down from 1.9 percent in 1995, and the statistics office said the economy stagnated in the final quarter, with virtually no growth from the third quarter.
German unemployment rose 48,000 to a seasonally adjusted 4.156 million in December, a new postwar record that topped the prior level of 4.1 million in November, the Federal Labour Office said.

On an unadjusted basis, 4.148 million were unemployed, below the peak of 4.27 million in February 1996. Federal Labour Office President Bernhard Jagoda said he could not rule out the unadjusted figure soon reaching 4.5 million.
The GDP rise was at the lower end of economists' expectations, while the jobless data were in line.
The news fuelled speculation that German interest rates, on hold since late last August, may be trimmed again and helped push the dollar up to a two-year high against the mark.
But the Bundesbank, which has repeatedly said rates are already low enough for an economic upturn, kept its key interest rates unchanged at Thursday's regular council meeting.

Economists said the figures showed Germany trapped in a vicious circle of mounting unemployment and weak growth, a dangerous combination as it enters 1997, the year on whose data candidates for currency union will be judged.

Under the EU stability pact thrashed out at Germany's insistence to ensure a strong Euro, Bonn would face a fine of 11 billion marks ($7 billion) for its deficit overshoot in 1996, said Joachim Fels, an economist at Morgan Stanley in London.

"The figures show we have a structural problem here and (Finance Minister Theo) Waigel's pledge to push the deficit below 3 percent in 1997 does not seem very credible to me," said Fels, who expects a deficit of 3.3 percent to 3.4 percent.
"I don't think monetary union will fail just because of an overshoot by a few decimal points but the overshoot will raise doubts about the credibility of the single currency," he added.
Despite the data, Chancellor Helmut Kohl said he saw good chances for an economic upturn, in part because of low inflation and low interest rates.
"We have no reason at all to talk negatively (about the economy)," Kohl told a news conference in Bonn. "The weak phase has been overcome ... The chances for an upturn have a solid foundation."
Kohl said he was ready to meet with company and union leaders to try to defeat the unemployment crisis, calling current levels "completely unacceptable."
"Fighting unemployment remains the most important domestic policy challenge," Kohl said.
